title: Structurally Separated DAG Learning with Multi-Scale Normalized Closure
claim: Pooled scalar objectives suffer three distinct biases, each with a targeted structural fix.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, each with a bias cartoon and a green fix box
description: Three side-by-side panels titled (a) Length-bias, (b) Multiplicity-bias and (c) Magnitude-bias. Each panel has a small graph cartoon with open circle nodes and colored arrows. Panel (a) shows a five-node directed cycle labeled L=5, with one thick orange edge and the rest blue. The caption below says the raw product shrinks as the cycle lengthens. Panel (b) shows a three-node cycle with a dashed orange curved arrow in the middle. The caption says the cycle re-enters at every walk length. Panel (c) shows two separate edges. A thick orange edge is labeled 'large |w| dominates A', and a thin blue edge is labeled 'small |w|: weak pressure'. Orange text marks each problem and blue marks the weak or normal case. Each panel ends with a rounded green box that states the fix. The fixes are length-normalized path scores, a strongest-path max-plus limit, and cycle pressure on the gate G instead of the weighted A. The eye goes first to the bold titles, then to the cycles.
caption: Effects that can arise when weighted-walk evidence is pooled into scalar acyclicity objectives, and corresponding design choices in our matrix-valued closure head: scale-normalized path scores mitigate length-dependent attenuation, the hard max-plus strongest-path limit reduces multiplicity from repeated traversals, and supervising the gate G rather than coefficient magnitudes in A = Wf(M) ⊙G(Z) separates structural support from effect size.
abstract: Continuous DAG learning commonly enforces acyclicity through scalar functions of a weighted adjacency that aggregate evidence from weighted closed walks. We add a complementary layer: matrix-valued closure logits---explicit multi-hop structural relation scores for each ordered pair---supervised alongside data fit, sparsity, and a DAGMA-style barrier on the weighted adjacency. The distinction is not scalarization of the overall objective but how path evidence is represented and exposed before aggregation. SMNC (scale-normalized multi-scale closure) builds these scores on a structural gate by repeated squaring in log space and divides each scale by its path-length budget, counteracting product-style attenuation along long cycles; diagonal entries support node-wise cycle supervision and off-diagonals optional pairwise reachability cues. In the linear model, a bounded structure--magnitude factorization ties strong effective edges to strong gates; a nonlinear induced gate offers another construction with the same intent. For sufficiently strong cycles, normalized logits admit a length-independent lower bound; under a unique-active-cycle assumption, the hard final-scale readout yields a polynomial log-gate gradient factor rather than exponential product-style decay. On cue-free, unstandardized Gaussian linear and nonlinear ER benchmarks, these models improve over DAGMA, run with default hyperparameters at a reduced budget, on denser graphs and are close to it on sparse ones.
